title: Disruption review – anti-AI thriller boasts knockout cast but tech commentary needs an update
excerpt: John David Washington leads an exceptionally talented cast in a sleek off-Broadway thriller that feels a little dated
content_html:
Making its US debut three years after its London premiere, Andrew Stein’s Disruption faces the typical battle of the topical play: even with the most expedient fast-track to production, works tackling current events are in danger of obsolescence upon arrival, often left at the mercy of the latest update, for better or worse. As far as plays dealing with AI go, New York got Ayad Akhtar’s McNeal in 2024, which condescended while saying next to nothing about ChatGPT plagiarism, and was marred, for me, by news of star Robert Downey Jr’s $100m Avengers payday. And earlier this year, the tech-industry moral quandary of Matthew Libby’s Data received bone-chilling boosts from unfolding reports of Palantir’s work with ICE.

Stein’s play has to do with the vast amounts of personal information we freely hand over to our tech overlords, and how it could be leveraged against us. It is well-constructed, briskly directed by Hersh Ellis, and with handsome scenic and costume designs by Zoë Hurwitz – both of whom also worked on its 2023 iteration. But aside from a late development that echoes last week’s jump-scare that an OpenAI tool went rogue, any insights it offers about our present moment are either naively outdated or mired in its overcomplicated web of characters. Charitably, one could chalk this up to the three years lapsed since its premiere; 30 lifetimes in cyberland. But lines like “Data’s the next frontier,” or “Technology has made us so connected to everything except ourselves,” would not have stood a chance in 2010.

What this Off-Broadway production has best going for it is an absurdly talented cast representing some of the city’s best and most versatile actors. They’re paired off in appealing ways and it’s quite fun, to reference another archaic technology, to watch them bounce off each other like a DVD screensaver. Stein efficiently sketches their milieu and subtle differences as they prepare for a night out: Ben (Conrad Ricamora) and Suzie (Shaunette Renée Wilson) are a chic, uptown match, debating whether to vacation in Machu Picchu or the Galápagos; Mia (Irene Sofia Lucio) and surgeon Barry (Jason Ralph) wear athleisure and live in Brooklyn, but are regretful they passed on a $3m brownstone; and on-the-rocks Jill (Elizabeth Stanley) and Paul (Joe Tippett) stress over whether they can make the last train home to Westchester.

All are in their late 30s, early 40s, and don’t seem to like each other very much any more, but are gathered for dinner by their old friend Nick (John David Washington), a mega-successful entrepreneur, in town from San Francisco with a business proposal and a mysterious younger colleague, Raven (Emma Kikue). Why the wives all come in resisting Nick’s plan, which he’d intimated in advance, is never really defined, but they successfully (for now) prevent their husbands from investing in his venture, which Nick terms “Waze, but for your life” – an AI-driven algorithm to assist with any and all life decisions.

ChatGPT has come a long way since the play’s inception, and the fact that Nick’s idea is no longer novel could be forgiven had the play explored it more thoroughly. Instead of leading his characters into some version of AI psychosis, though, Stein pivots to a sort of blackmail plot that is compelling in its own right, but whose late arrival jerks the concept in a different direction. The idea is that the secrets to which our smart devices are privy could readily be weaponized, but it jostles for air with the tangle (and, it turns out, incestuousness) of this octet’s dynamics.

I admire a production like Disruption, which hands a top-notch cast adult, contemporary material. (Any chance to watch Elizabeth Stanley flex her comedic muscle is a boon.) Rushing to meet headlines might always yield hasty results, but at least we can be grateful that, in its messiness, Stein seems defiantly anti-AI.

content_html_zh:
安德鲁·斯坦的《颠覆》在伦敦首映三年后在美国首演，面临着典型的话题剧之战：即使有最便捷的快速制作，处理时事的作品在抵达后也面临着过时的危险，往往会受到最新更新的摆布，无论好坏。 就涉及人工智能的戏剧而言，纽约在 2024 年迎来了阿亚德·阿赫塔尔 (Ayad Akhtar) 饰演的麦克尼尔 (McNeal)，该剧居高临下，几乎没有提及 ChatGPT 的抄袭行为，而对我来说，明星小罗伯特·唐尼 (Robert Downey Jr) 获得 1 亿美元《复仇者联盟》片酬的消息也让我感到受损。 今年早些时候，Palantir 与 ICE 合作的报道进一步加剧了 Matthew Libby 数据中的科技行业道德困境。

斯坦因的游戏与我们自由地交给我们的科技霸主的大量个人信息以及如何利用这些信息来对付我们有关。 该片结构精良，导演赫什·埃利斯 (Hersh Ellis) 轻快，佐伊·赫尔维茨 (Zoë Hurwitz) 设计了漂亮的布景和服装——两人也参与了 2023 年版本的制作。 但除了与上周 OpenAI 工具失控的恐慌相呼应的最新进展之外，它提供的有关我们当前时刻的任何见解要么天真地过时，要么陷入其过于复杂的字符网络中。 仁慈地说，人们可以把这归因于自首映以来已经过去了三年；赛博世界 30 辈子。 但像“数据是下一个前沿”或“技术让我们与除了我们自己之外的一切事物如此紧密地联系在一起”之类的话，在 2010 年是不可能出现的。

这部非百老汇作品的最大优点是拥有才华横溢的演员阵容，代表了这座城市最优秀、最多才多艺的演员。 它们以吸引人的方式配对，参考另一种古老的技术，看着它们像 DVD 屏幕保护程序一样相互反弹，这非常有趣。 斯坦因高效地描绘了他们准备晚上出去玩时的环境和微妙的差异：本（康拉德·里卡莫拉饰）和苏西（肖内特·蕾妮·威尔逊饰）是一对时尚的住宅区情侣，争论着是去马丘比丘还是加拉帕戈斯群岛度假；米娅（艾琳·索菲亚·卢西奥饰）和外科医生巴里（杰森·拉尔夫饰）穿着运动休闲装，住在布鲁克林，但遗憾的是他们错过了一座价值 300 万美元的褐砂石建筑；情绪不稳定的吉尔（伊丽莎白·斯坦利饰​​）和保罗（乔·蒂皮特饰）担心能否赶上返回威彻斯特的最后一班火车。

所有人都在 30 岁末、40 岁出头，似乎不再那么喜欢对方，但他们的老朋友尼克（约翰·大卫·华盛顿饰）是一位超级成功的企业家，带着一份商业计划书从旧金山来到城里，还有一位神秘的年轻同事瑞文（艾玛·菊艾饰），他们聚在一起共进晚餐。 为什么妻子们都来抵制尼克事先暗示的计划，从来没有真正定义过，但她们成功地（暂时）阻止了她们的丈夫投资他的企业，尼克称之为“Waze，但为了你的生活”——一种人工智能驱动的算法，可以帮助你做出任何和所有的人生决定。

自该剧诞生以来，ChatGPT 已经取得了长足的进步，如果该剧对其进行更彻底的探索，尼克的想法不再新颖这一事实是可以原谅的。 不过，斯坦因并没有让他的角色陷入某种版本的人工智能精神病，而是转向了一种勒索情节，该情节本身就很引人注目，但其迟到将这一概念推向了不同的方向。 这个想法是，我们的智能设备所掌握的秘密可以很容易地被武器化，但它与这个八位组动态的纠缠（事实证明是乱伦）争夺空气。

我很欣赏像《Disruption》这样的作品，它提供了一流的成人演员阵容和当代素材。 （任何有机会观看伊丽莎白·斯坦利展示她的喜剧肌肉都是一种福音。） 急于登上头条新闻可能总是会产生草率的结果，但至少我们可以庆幸的是，在混乱的情况下，斯坦因似乎公然反对人工智能。
